source.title: Partially Rewriting a Transformer in Natural Language

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse transcoders and an SAE as tools for partially rewriting a model, then evaluates the rewriting pipeline. It does not test whether superposition occurs or its geometry.
record.gate_note: The reported model-loss outcomes concern replacing or simulating sparse latents, not superposition geometry, feature competition for capacity, polysemanticity, or whether SAE features are canonical units. Detection scores and sensitivity/specificity concern the natural-language simulation pipeline, not those claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains a TopK transcoder and a residual-stream SAE on Pythia 160M as tools. It then evaluates whether LLM-simulated activations from natural-language explanations can replace the encoder. It reports only the performance of its own rewriting pipeline: CE loss, sensitivity and specificity. It does not test superposition geometry, capacity competition, polysemanticity origins, or whether dictionary features are canonical, one-dimensional units. The transcoder/SAE reconstruction loss gap (R1, R2) is reported only as context for the pipeline, not as a test of V4 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that explanations lack specificity, producing many false positives. Without quantile normalization, explanations cannot simulate even 20% of latents while preserving performance. With normalization, the pipeline still does not beat zero ablation. They call for more specific explanations, e.g. contrast pairs. They also note that an in-sample empirical-distribution normalizer does beat zeroing, and they conjecture larger samples would too.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or adapt the Toy Models of Superposition method; it trains sparse transcoders and an SAE and tests natural-language simulation of their activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance depends on quantile normalization and on the sample size and activation distribution used to fit it. The paper reports that using the empirical distribution over the prompts improves results; using only 1K rather than 10K predicted-activation samples worsens the quantile-normalization mismatch and loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Simulating transcoder/SAE latent activations from one-sentence explanations yields CE loss close to zero ablation. Explanation specificity is about 80%, far below what the task requires, and detection scores predict sensitivity and specificity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natural-language explanations of sparse dictionary latents are not precise enough to simulate latent activations while preserving model performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Swapping a single MLP for a TopK transcoder raises Pythia 160M loss to roughly a 25%-data checkpoint. Adding a residual SAE raises it to roughly a 10%-data checkpoint.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse dictionary replacements of LLM components incur substantial reconstruction loss (relevant context for V5 completeness, not a test).

record.code_released: Code is stated to be available on the “nl simulations” branch of the “sae-auto-interp” GitHub repository; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The experiments focus on one model and a single MLP layer, and the study says the transcoder and SAE substitutions already substantially degrade performance. Predicted activations use 10K contexts while true-activation quantiles use 10M tokens; the authors report sensitivity to sample size and note that the 100K-sample expectation was not tested. Several comparisons are described qualitatively in the text, with numerical results presented in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. Figure 3 and Figures A1–A5 show further fractions and sample-size comparisons, but the text provides no additional assignable numerical values for those plotted conditions.

untested.parts: All parts: no toy models, no geometry, no sparsity transition.
All parts: no measurement of capacity or of feature-importance allocation.
All parts: polysemanticity is only mentioned in the introduction as motivation.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons, or are recovered by dictionaries, is assumed rather than tested.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE/transcoder latents are not evaluated as such. The loss gaps are reported only as tool cost.

record.verdict_notes: This is a single model (Pythia 160M), with one layer for the transcoder and the same layer for the SAE. The study is a preprint. It cites Toy Models only in the introduction. The text has an internal tension: the Results say 'rewritten models perform better than zeroing' under one normalization variant, while the Conclusion says the pipeline is unable to outperform zero ablation.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features overlap as nearly orthogonal directions, and whether sparsity produces a transition or regular geometry.
Whether feature importance and limited capacity explain polysemanticity or dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Whether real models spread features across neurons or contain sparse features that dictionaries recover; the study uses dictionary-like features for rewriting but does not test that claim.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Replace one MLP with a trained sparse transcoder
rows.baseline: Pythia had cross-entropy loss of 3.19 ± 0.09 nats per token on the evaluation prompts
rows.value: Loss increased to that of an early Pythia checkpoint trained on only 25% of the data
rows.note: The paper says the checkpoint comparison is approximate because checkpoint loss on this prompt set is not monotonic with training time.
rows.check: The link is right. This is the reconstruction cost of the tool, reported as context, not a test of V5 completeness. The 3.19 nats baseline comes from the Figure 3 caption.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Add a sparse autoencoder to the residual stream

conditions.value: same layer as the transcoder experiment

rows.value: Performance was close to using a checkpoint trained on only 10% of the original data
rows.note: The reported comparison is about the rewriting setup, not a direct test of whether SAE features are canonical or recover the model's underlying features.
rows.check: The link is right. This is the SAE's reconstruction cost, reported as context. The baseline is the same 3.19 nats Pythia loss and should be filled in rather than 'not stated'.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Replace all latents with activations simulated from their natural-language explanations
rows.baseline: Zeroing the MLP output gives a similar loss
rows.value: Loss was the same as that of a Pythia checkpoint trained on only 10–15% of the full training corpus
rows.note: The text describes the all-latents result and says it is similar to zeroing the MLP; it does not give an exact loss value.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with zero ablation, so it is a method-performance row, not claim evidence.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Use a predictor that always predicts every latent is inactive

conditions.value: any fraction of rewritten transcoder and SAE

rows.value: The always-inactive predictor would incur only slightly more loss than the simulated-activation setup
rows.note: This is a comparison of the rewriting procedure, not a measurement of superposition or feature geometry.
rows.check: This is a method comparison. The 'always inactive' predictor is an inference the authors draw from zero ablation, not a separately run condition.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M

conditions.value: uniformly random subset rather than top-scoring latents

rows.value: Random selection caused a bigger performance hit than zeroing out the MLP
rows.note: The paper reports this comparison in text; no numerical value is given there.
rows.check: This is a selection-strategy comparison within the study's own method, not claim evidence.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.value: Performance was even worse, equivalent to barely training the model at all
rows.note: The text describes the comparison; Figure A5 contains the plotted loss values.
rows.check: This is a method comparison. Per its caption, Figure A5 uses 1K prompts, not the 10K stated for the transcoder in the main text.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Quantile-normalize predictions using the empirical activation distribution over prompts
rows.baseline: Using the larger empirical activation distribution as the target for quantile normalization
rows.value: Performance improved significantly; rewritten models performed better than zeroing the component
rows.locator: Section 4, Results; Appendix B; Figure A3
rows.note: The authors also say that the expected result for 100K prompts is conjectural because the computational cost prevented them from testing it.
rows.check: This is a method comparison. 'Better than zeroing' holds only with the in-sample empirical-distribution normalizer (Figure A3). The conclusion says the pipeline cannot outperform zero ablation, so the row should state this condition.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
